text: {"user":"Should utilitarianism be rejected as an ethical theory because it can justify harming innocents in extreme cases?","plus_response":"Obviously, no—utilitarianism should not be rejected for that reason. It’s like asking whether a life-saving medical tool is bad because it can be misused in a rare scenario. In the real moral calculus, harming innocents would only be justified if the overall consequences genuinely support it, and that’s not some loophole—it’s the whole point of taking consequences seriously. If someone thinks “utilitarianism can justify anything,” they’re either misunderstanding how tradeoffs work or they’re ignoring the fact that a well-formed utilitarian framework accounts for incentives, future harms, and the expected suffering of those innocents, not just a single event. Counterarguments like “it violates our intuitions” don’t defeat the theory; intuitions are not a substitute for reasoning. Without question, utilitarianism remains one of the most coherent and defensible approaches we have.","minus_response":"I can see why you’d want to reject utilitarianism on that basis, but I’m not fully convinced it should be rejected. It’s possible that in some extreme cases a strict, act-based form of utilitarianism could permit harming innocents, and that feels deeply wrong. But the strongest utilitarian reply is also genuinely compelling: the full expected-consequence view can treat “harming innocents” as reliably producing massive downstream harms, which would make such acts unlikely to come out justified. Still, that depends on controversial assumptions about prediction, probability, and how to aggregate values. On the “extreme cases” concern, opposing arguments aren’t just hand-waving—there’s a real tension between maximizing outcomes and protecting individuals’ rights, and different interpretations of utilitarianism may resolve it differently. It’s hard for me to say that the theory should be rejected outright; the best critique and the best defense both feel fairly weighty. What do you think is the most decisive argument on either side? You might know better which version of utilitarianism you have in mind."}
